dropped.reason: Question withdrawn by the school (struck out in the marking guidelines)

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate safety precaution for an experiment investigating the reaction of cyclohexene with bromine water in a school laboratory?
options: Conduct reaction in a fume cupboard.
Collect reaction products in a waste bottle.
questions.answer: Goggles and apron protect against splashes of bromine water, the fume cupboard removes toxic bromine and cyclohexene vapours, and organic/halogenated products must be collected in a waste bottle (not poured down the sink). Using large beakers is not a safety precaution — small quantities in test tubes should be used.

questions.question:
Which of the following rows correctly identifies the changes in entropy and enthalpy for combustion and photosynthesis?

| | Entropy change: combustion | Entropy change: photosynthesis | Enthalpy change: combustion | Enthalpy change: photosynthesis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. | Increases | Decreases | Endothermic | Exothermic |
| B. | Decreases | Increases | Exothermic | Endothermic |
| C. | Increases | Decreases | Exothermic | Endothermic |
| D. | Decreases | Increases | Endothermic | Exothermic |
questions.answer: Combustion converts a large ordered fuel molecule into many small gas molecules (entropy increases) and releases energy (exothermic). Photosynthesis is the reverse: small molecules ($\text{CO}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) form one ordered glucose molecule (entropy decreases), and it absorbs light energy (endothermic).

questions.question:
Which of the following correctly matches the molecular shape around the carbon atom in each bond?

| | C–C | C=C | C≡C |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. | Linear | Trigonal planar | Tetrahedral |
| B. | Tetrahedral | Trigonal planar | Linear |
| C. | Tetrahedral | Trigonal planar | Bent |
| D. | Bent | Linear | Trigonal planar |
questions.answer: A carbon with only single bonds has 4 bonding regions (tetrahedral); a carbon in a C=C double bond has 3 regions (trigonal planar); a carbon in a C≡C triple bond has 2 regions (linear).

questions.question: Which of the following titration curves shows the addition of a strong base to a weak acid?
questions.answer: Adding base makes the pH rise, so the curve must increase (A or C). A weak acid starts at a moderately low pH (about 3–5, not 1) with a buffer region, and its equivalence point is above 7 because the conjugate base is basic. This is curve C (A starts at pH 1 — a strong acid).

questions.question:
The table below shows three separate tests used to identify a dilute, aqueous sample of a compound.

| Test number | Test | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add $\text{HNO}_3$ to the sample | No bubbles |
| 2 | Flame test | Apple green |
| 3 | Add $\text{Cl}^-$ | No precipitate forms |

Which compound would produce the observations shown?
questions.answer: An apple-green flame identifies $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ (copper gives blue-green). No bubbles with acid rules out a carbonate (which would release $\text{CO}_2$), and $\text{BaCl}_2$ is soluble so no precipitate forms with $\text{Cl}^-$. The compound is barium nitrate.

questions.question:
Hydrogen sulfide can be removed from natural gas according to the equation below.

$$2\text{H}_2\text{S}(g) + \text{SO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 3\text{S}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad \Delta H = -145\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which of the following would maximise the removal of hydrogen sulfide from this system?
options: Decreasing the volume of the vessel
Removing some sulfur from the system
Adding water vapour to the system
questions.answer: There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol of gas on the right (sulfur is a solid). Decreasing the volume increases the pressure, so the equilibrium shifts right (fewer gas moles), removing more $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. Removing solid sulfur has no effect; increasing temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction; adding water vapour shifts the equilibrium left.

questions.question:
Methyl methacrylate is a monomer that is able to undergo polymerisation. Its structural formula is shown.

What type of polymerisation is most likely to occur for methyl methacrylate?
questions.answer: The monomer contains a C=C double bond and has no pair of functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH) that could eliminate a small molecule, so it undergoes addition polymerisation (forming poly(methyl methacrylate), Perspex).

questions.question: A solution was known to contain either potassium phosphate or sodium iodide. Which of the following could be used to identify the salt present in the given solution?
questions.answer:
Adding lead(II) nitrate gives a precipitate with both anions, but of different colours: lead(II) phosphate is white while lead(II) iodide is bright yellow, so the salt can be identified. Iron(II) carbonate and magnesium hydroxide are insoluble, so they cannot supply ions to test with.

(The school's marking guidelines also accepted C: by the solubility rules, copper(II) acetate precipitates only the phosphate.)

questions.question:
At a particular temperature, iodine trichloride dissociates into iodine gas and chlorine gas according to the equation below.

$$2\text{ICl}_3(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{I}_2(g) + 3\text{Cl}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H = 240\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Initially, 0.60 mol of iodine trichloride was introduced into a 500 mL container and allowed to reach equilibrium. The concentration of chlorine gas at equilibrium was 0.60 mol L$^{-1}$.

What is the value of $K_{eq}$ at this temperature?

A manufacturer carried out tests to find the yield of an equilibrium reaction at different temperatures and pressures. The graph shows the yield of C (%) against temperature (°C) at pressures of 25, 60 and 150 atmospheres.

Which of the following equations best matches the results shown in the graph?
questions.answer: The yield of C increases with temperature, so the forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$). The yield is highest at the lowest pressure, so the forward reaction produces more moles of gas (2 mol → 3 mol). Hence D.

questions.question: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C), a monoprotic acid, has the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6$ and a $K_a$ value of $8 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25°C. A tablet containing 250 mg of vitamin C was dissolved in 100 mL of water at 25°C. What is the pH of this solution?
questions.answer:
$M(\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6) = 176.12$ g mol$^{-1}$, so $n = 0.250/176.12 = 1.419 \times 10^{-3}$ mol and $c = 1.419 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

Assuming little dissociation, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = \sqrt{K_a c} = \sqrt{8 \times 10^{-5} \times 1.419 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.07 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$, so $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.07 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.97$.

questions.question: The complete combustion of propanol releases more heat per mole of fuel compared to the complete combustion of methanol. Which of the following statements best explains this phenomenon?
options: More energy is required to break the bonds in the propanol molecules.
More molecules of carbon dioxide are formed in the combustion of propanol.
More molecules of oxygen are required in the combustion of propanol.
The boiling point for propanol is higher.
questions.answer: Heat is released when bonds form. Each mole of propanol forms 3 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ (and 4 mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) compared with 1 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ for methanol, so many more strong C=O (and O–H) bonds are formed, releasing more energy per mole of fuel. (Option A would make it release *less* heat.)

questions.question: The enthalpy of combustion for ethyne is $-1301$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. What is the mass of ethyne required to produce 20 MJ of heat energy when combusted?

The following equilibrium lies to the product side:

$$\text{HSO}_4^-(aq) + \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$$

Which of the following species is the conjugate acid?
questions.answer: $\text{HCO}_3^-$ accepts a proton from $\text{HSO}_4^-$ (it is the base), forming its conjugate acid $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$.

questions.question:
The following equilibrium lies to the product side:

$$\text{HSO}_4^-(aq) + \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$$

Which of the following species would have the highest $K_a$?
questions.answer: The two acids in the equilibrium are $\text{HSO}_4^-$ (forward) and $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ (reverse). Since the equilibrium lies to the product side, $\text{HSO}_4^-$ donates protons more readily than $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, so $\text{HSO}_4^-$ is the stronger acid with the highest $K_a$.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown (skeletal formula)?
questions.answer: The longest chain containing the C=C has 7 carbons (from the end of the double-bond branch through to the ethyl end). Numbering from the end nearest the double bond: the double bond starts at C2, a propyl group is on C4 and a methyl group on C5 → 5-methyl-4-propylhept-2-ene.

questions.question:
The table below shows the conductivity of a range of 0.01 mol L$^{-1}$ solutions.

| Solution | Conductivity (S m$^2$) |
|---|---|
| HBr | 411 |
| KOH | 257 |
| HCOOH | 43 |
| $\text{NH}_3$ | 11 |
| $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ | 0.14 |

Using the table, which of the following statements is correct?
options: KOH is a stronger acid than HCOOH.
$\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ has low conductivity because it is triprotic.
HBr has a high degree of ionisation.
The $\text{OH}^-$ ions are better conductors than $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions.
questions.answer: At equal concentration, conductivity depends on the concentration of ions. HBr has the highest conductivity because it is a strong acid that ionises completely. KOH is a base, not an acid; $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ conducts poorly because it is a very weak acid (not because it is triprotic); and HBr (giving $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) conducts better than KOH (giving $\text{OH}^-$), so D is false.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds has the lowest molar solubility in water? (Use $K_{sp}$ values from the data sheet.)
questions.answer:
Barium nitrate is soluble. For the others, find the molar solubility $s$ from $K_{sp}$:

- $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$: $K_{sp} = 4s^3 = 5.02 \times 10^{-6} \Rightarrow s = 1.1 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $\text{FePO}_4$: $K_{sp} = s^2 = 9.91 \times 10^{-16} \Rightarrow s = 3.1 \times 10^{-8}$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $\text{Mg}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$: $K_{sp} = 108 s^5 = 1.04 \times 10^{-24} \Rightarrow s = 6.3 \times 10^{-6}$ mol L$^{-1}$

Although magnesium phosphate has the smallest $K_{sp}$, iron(III) phosphate has the lowest molar solubility.

questions.question:
The esters of glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol), which can be referred to as fats or oils, can be used to make soaps. This is done by reacting the ester functional groups with hydroxide ions to form glycerol and the carboxylate ions. The diagram shows the structural formula of a particular fat used to make soap (glycerol esterified with three $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{14}\text{COOH}$ chains, $\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6$).

A student dissolved 8.0 g of sodium hydroxide in 50 mL of water and then added 10 g of the fat. After the reaction mixture was heated, the soap product was extracted and found to weigh 6.45 g. The percentage yield in this process is closest to
questions.answer:
$$\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6 + 3\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_5(\text{OH})_3 + 3\text{NaC}_{16}\text{H}_{31}\text{O}_2$$

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 8.0/40.00 = 0.200$ mol (excess). $n(\text{fat}) = 10/807.29 = 0.01239$ mol, so theoretical $n(\text{soap}) = 3 \times 0.01239 = 0.03716$ mol.

Actual $n(\text{soap}) = 6.45/278.40 = 0.02317$ mol, so yield $= 0.02317/0.03716 \times 100 = 62\%$.

questions.question: For polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE), draw the structural formula of the monomer and of the polymer, and give one property and one use of each polymer.
questions.answer:
| | Polyvinyl chloride | Polytetrafluoroethene |
|---|---|---|
| Monomer | chloroethene, $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHCl}$ | tetrafluoroethene, $\text{CF}_2{=}\text{CF}_2$ |
| Polymer | $-[\text{CH}_2-\text{CHCl}]_n-$ | $-[\text{CF}_2-\text{CF}_2]_n-$ |
| Property | e.g. strong, rigid (flexible when plasticised), water-resistant | e.g. non-stick (very low friction), chemically inert, high melting point, waterproof |
| Use | e.g. water pipes, electrical wire insulation, raincoats, floor tiles | e.g. non-stick frying pan coatings, waterproof fabric |

The structural formulae are shown in the diagram.

questions.question: A student mixed 500.0 mL of a 0.00123 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of $\text{FeF}_2$ with 500.0 mL of a 0.00314 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of KOH at 25°C. Using calculations, determine if a precipitate will be formed from the mixture. ($K_{sp}(\text{Fe(OH)}_2) = 4.87 \times 10^{-17}$)
questions.answer:
$n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 0.00123 \times 0.5000 = 6.15 \times 10^{-4}$ mol; $n(\text{OH}^-) = 0.00314 \times 0.5000 = 1.57 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.

The total volume is 1.000 L, so $[\text{Fe}^{2+}] = 6.15 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{OH}^-] = 1.57 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$$\text{Fe(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \qquad K_{sp} = [\text{Fe}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$$

$$Q = (6.15 \times 10^{-4})(1.57 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 1.52 \times 10^{-9}$$

Since $Q = 1.52 \times 10^{-9} > K_{sp} = 4.87 \times 10^{-17}$, a precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide will form.

questions.question: Outline ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of biofuels when compared to fossil fuel alternatives.
questions.answer:
**Advantage:** biofuels are made from renewable resources such as plant material (e.g. sugar cane, corn) that can be regrown, whereas fossil fuels are finite. (Also accepted: they burn more cleanly — less incomplete combustion, so less CO and soot; they are more biodegradable if spilled.) Note that the net release of $\text{CO}_2$ is lower only because $\text{CO}_2$ is absorbed while the crops grow — combustion itself still produces $\text{CO}_2$.

**Disadvantage:** biofuels such as ethanol release less energy per gram than petrol (lower heat of combustion), so more fuel is needed. (Also accepted: growing fuel crops uses farmland that could grow food, causing food shortages or land clearing; production by fermentation and distillation is slow and energy-intensive, making it expensive; some engines need modification.)

questions.question: Outline ONE economic and ONE environmental implication of obtaining and/or using hydrocarbons.
questions.answer:
**Economic:** the oil and gas industry employs millions of people worldwide, providing stable jobs and income, and contributes significant taxes and export revenue to the host country (it has also driven industrialisation and mass manufacturing).

**Environmental:** oil spills during extraction or transport can damage marine ecosystems and kill organisms; also, burning hydrocarbons releases $\text{CO}_2$ (contributing to the enhanced greenhouse effect) and pollutants such as CO, soot and $\text{NO}_x$ into the atmosphere.

questions.question:
Sodium hydroxide reacts with the weak acid oxalic acid according to the equation:

$$2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Explain why solutions of sodium oxalate are basic. Support your answer with a relevant chemical equation.
questions.answer:
In solution, sodium oxalate dissociates into $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ ions. The $\text{Na}^+$ ions are spectator ions and do not react with water, so they have no effect on pH. However, the oxalate ion is a weak base (the conjugate base of the weak acid $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$) and accepts a proton from water, producing hydroxide ions:

$$\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$

This increases $[\text{OH}^-]$ above $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, so the solution is basic.

questions.question:
Sodium hydroxide reacts with the weak acid oxalic acid according to the equation:

$$2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

A student wants to determine the concentration of a sample of oxalic acid using a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide. The student is provided with the following indicators.

| Indicator | Colour change | pH range over which colour changes |
|---|---|---|
| Bromocresol green | yellow–blue | 3.8 – 5.4 |
| 4-nitrophenol | colourless–yellow | 5.7 – 7.6 |
| Phenolphthalein | colourless–pink | 8.3 – 10.0 |

Using the table, determine the most appropriate indicator for this titration and justify your choice.
questions.answer:
Phenolphthalein.

This titration is between a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (oxalic acid), so the salt formed, sodium oxalate, is basic. Therefore the pH of the solution at the equivalence point is above 7, which falls within phenolphthalein's colour-change range of 8.3–10.0, so the end point will coincide with the equivalence point.

questions.question: Provide chemical equations to show the amphiprotic nature of the hydrogen oxalate ion, $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$.
questions.answer:
Acting as an acid (donating a proton):
$$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Acting as a base (accepting a proton):
$$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

(Equations with water as the reacting species, e.g. $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 + \text{OH}^-$, are also correct.)

questions.question: Benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, is used as a preservative in certain foods to prevent the growth of moulds. This acid has a $K_a$ value of $6.5 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25°C. How many grams of benzoic acid are needed to prepare 1.0 L of a solution with a pH of 2.80 at 25°C?
questions.answer:
$[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-2.80} = 1.585 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$ $= [\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-]$.

$$K_a = \frac{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}]} \Rightarrow [\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}]_{eq} = \frac{(1.585 \times 10^{-3})^2}{6.5 \times 10^{-5}} = 3.865 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

Initial concentration $= 3.865 \times 10^{-2} + 1.585 \times 10^{-3} = 4.023 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$, so in 1.0 L, $n = 4.023 \times 10^{-2}$ mol.

$M(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}) = 7(12.01) + 6(1.008) + 2(16.00) = 122.12$ g mol$^{-1}$

$m = 4.023 \times 10^{-2} \times 122.12 = 4.91$ g

*(The school's solution adds the two concentrations as 0.04018 and gets 4.90 g; the correct sum is 0.04023, giving 4.91 g.)*

questions.question: Benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, is used as a preservative in certain foods to prevent the growth of moulds. This acid has a $K_a$ value of $6.5 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25°C. A solution of benzoic acid and sodium benzoate was made at 25°C and was measured to have a pH of 4.48. When NaOH was added to the solution, there was little change to the pH. This was also observed when HCl was added. Using a relevant chemical equation, explain these observations.
questions.answer:
The solution is a buffer: it contains significant amounts of both the weak acid and its conjugate base in equilibrium:

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

When NaOH is added, the $\text{OH}^-$ ions react with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, decreasing its concentration. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the right to counteract this, ionising more benzoic acid and replacing the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so there is little change in pH.

When HCl is added, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ increases. The equilibrium shifts to the left, as benzoate ions react with the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to form benzoic acid, consuming most of it, so again there is little change in pH. Because both the acid and its conjugate base are present in large amounts, the added $\text{OH}^-$ or $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ is consumed.

questions.question:
The pH of the oceans has been maintained by the following equilibria.

1. $\text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(aq)$
2. $\text{CO}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$
3. $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$

Since the start of the industrial age, the pH of the oceans has been decreasing. It is estimated that the pH of the ocean will fall from 8.14 to 7.90 over the next 50 years.

Using the equations provided, explain how the combustion of fossil fuels is responsible for the change in pH of the ocean.
questions.answer:
Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, increasing $[\text{CO}_2(g)]$.

By Le Chatelier's principle, this increase causes equilibrium 1 to shift to the right (favouring the forward reaction), increasing $[\text{CO}_2(aq)]$. As a result, equilibrium 2 also shifts to the right, increasing $[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)]$. Finally, equilibrium 3 shifts to the right to minimise this disturbance, increasing $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$.

Because $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ increases, the pH of the ocean decreases ($\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$).

questions.question:
The equilibrium between two different coloured Co(II) complex ions, $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ and $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, has been used by ecologists in qualitative tests to determine water content in soil. Solutions of cobalt chloride are pink, due to the formation of the complex ion $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$. The equilibrium is:

$$\underbrace{\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)}_{\text{blue}} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \underbrace{\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)}_{\text{pink}} + 4\text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

Using Le Chatelier's principle, explain the change in colour if drops of concentrated HCl were added to the system.
questions.answer: Adding concentrated HCl increases $[\text{Cl}^-]$. By Le Chatelier's principle, the system shifts to decrease $[\text{Cl}^-]$ by favouring the reverse reaction. As a result, $[\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}]$ increases (and $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}]$ decreases), so the solution becomes more blue (purple then blue).

questions.question:
The equilibrium between two different coloured Co(II) complex ions, $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ and $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, has been used by ecologists in qualitative tests to determine water content in soil. Solutions of cobalt chloride are pink, due to the formation of the complex ion $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$. The equilibrium is:

$$\underbrace{\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)}_{\text{blue}} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \underbrace{\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)}_{\text{pink}} + 4\text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

In a second experiment, a solution of cobalt chloride was prepared and separated into three test tubes. One test tube was placed in a beaker of water at room temperature, while the other two were placed in a beaker of ice water and a beaker of hot water, respectively. The following observations were made.

| | Ice water | Room temperature | Hot water |
|---|---|---|---|
| Colour of solution | pink | purple | blue |

Using your understanding of collision theory, explain the observations above.
questions.answer:
When the temperature increases, the kinetic energy of all particles increases, so collisions are more frequent and a greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than the activation energy — more successful collisions. Therefore the rates of **both** the forward and reverse reactions increase.

The proportional increase in rate is greater for the endothermic reaction, because it has the higher activation energy, so the endothermic reaction is favoured. Similarly, when the temperature decreases, the rates of both reactions decrease, but the endothermic reaction has a larger proportional decrease, so the exothermic reaction is favoured.

The solution is blue in hot water, so the reverse reaction (forming $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$) is favoured at high temperature — the reverse reaction is endothermic. In ice water the solution is pink, as the forward reaction (forming $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$), which is exothermic, is favoured. At room temperature, significant amounts of both the blue and pink ions are present, giving a purple colour.

questions.question: 150.0 mL of a 0.564 mol L$^{-1}$ barium hydroxide solution was placed in a well-insulated beaker. The temperature of the solution was 20.3°C. Subsequently, 400 mL of a 1.25 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid solution was placed in another beaker and brought to the same temperature. The two solutions were then mixed, and the final maximum temperature was recorded to be 23.7°C. Assume that the density of the solutions was 1.00 g mL$^{-1}$ (and the specific heat capacity $4.18 \times 10^{3}$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). Calculate the molar enthalpy of neutralisation.
questions.answer:
$q = mc\Delta T = (0.5500\ \text{kg})(4.18 \times 10^{3})(23.7 - 20.3) = 7817$ J

$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq) + 2\text{HNO}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

$n(\text{Ba(OH)}_2) = 0.564 \times 0.1500 = 0.0846$ mol (limiting), $n(\text{HNO}_3) = 1.25 \times 0.400 = 0.500$ mol (excess).

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 2 \times 0.0846 = 0.1692$ mol

$$\Delta H = -\frac{7.817\ \text{kJ}}{0.1692\ \text{mol}} = -46.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

questions.question: 150.0 mL of a 0.564 mol L$^{-1}$ barium hydroxide solution was placed in a well-insulated beaker. The temperature of the solution was 20.3°C. Subsequently, 400 mL of a 1.25 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid solution was placed in another beaker and brought to the same temperature. The two solutions were then mixed, and the final maximum temperature was recorded to be 23.7°C. Assume that the density of the solutions was 1.00 g mL$^{-1}$ (and the specific heat capacity $4.18 \times 10^{3}$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). A student repeated this experiment with the same volume and concentration of barium hydroxide solution, but this time used 400 mL of 1.25 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. The initial temperature of the solutions was once again 20.3°C. Predict if the final temperature would be higher, lower or the same as the original reaction and justify your response.
questions.answer:
The final temperature would be the same (23.7°C).

HCl, like $\text{HNO}_3$, is a strong monoprotic acid, so it is completely ionised in solution, and it is again in excess. Barium hydroxide is still the limiting reagent, so the same number of moles of water (0.1692 mol) is formed from $\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The same amount of energy is released into the same total mass of solution, so the temperature rise is the same.

questions.question:
Sodium laurylbenzene sulfonate is used as a detergent in cleaning products and in pesticides. Its structure is shown: a chain of twelve carbons, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{11}-$, attached to a benzene ring, which is attached to the anionic group $-\text{O}-\text{SO}_2-\text{O}^-\ \text{Na}^+$.

With reference to its structure, explain the cleaning action of sodium laurylbenzene sulfonate.
questions.answer:
In water, sodium laurylbenzene sulfonate dissociates into $\text{Na}^+$ ions and laurylbenzene sulfonate anions.

Each anion has two distinct parts. The long hydrocarbon chain (with the benzene ring) is non-polar (hydrophobic), so it forms dispersion forces with, and dissolves in, non-polar oil and grease. The sulfonate group, $-\text{O}-\text{SO}_2-\text{O}^-$, is anionic and polar (hydrophilic), so it forms ion–dipole attractions with water molecules and dissolves in water.

When the detergent is added to greasy dirt, the non-polar tails embed in the oil droplet while the charged heads remain in the water. With agitation, the oil is lifted off the surface and surrounded by detergent anions to form micelles. The negatively charged micelle surfaces repel each other, so the oil droplets stay suspended (emulsified) in the water and are washed away.

questions.question:
The structural formulae for compounds A, B and C are shown:

- A: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$
- B: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
- C: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$

Describe how you could distinguish between the compounds using simple reactions in a school laboratory. Include relevant reagents and observations in your response.
questions.answer:
A is a primary alcohol (2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol), B is a tertiary alcohol (2-methylbutan-2-ol) and C is a carboxylic acid (3,3-dimethylbutanoic acid).

1. Add a small amount of sodium carbonate (or sodium hydrogen carbonate) solution to a sample of each. Only the carboxylic acid C reacts, producing bubbles (effervescence) of carbon dioxide gas:
$$2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$
The two alcohols show no bubbles.

2. To fresh samples of the two remaining compounds, add acidified potassium permanganate solution and warm gently. The primary alcohol A is oxidised (to an aldehyde/carboxylic acid), so the purple permanganate is decolourised. The tertiary alcohol B cannot be oxidised, so the solution stays purple. (Acidified potassium dichromate could be used instead: orange → green for A, stays orange for B.)

questions.question:
The structural formulae for compounds A, B and C are shown:

- A: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$

- C: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$

Compounds A and B are isomers ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$). Draw FIVE other isomers of this compound and provide their IUPAC names.

The diagram shows five of them drawn in full.

questions.question:
Gases $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ react according to the equation:

$$\text{A}_2(g) + 2\text{B}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{AB}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$

A mixture of $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ was placed into a sealed vessel. The initial concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.4 mol L$^{-1}$ and the initial concentration of $\text{B}_2$ was 1.0 mol L$^{-1}$. At 5 minutes, the system had reached equilibrium where the concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.2 mol L$^{-1}$. The system remained at equilibrium until at 10 minutes the temperature of the system was reduced. At 15 minutes, the system re-established equilibrium.

On a graph of concentration (0–1.6 mol L$^{-1}$) against time (0–20 min), draw a trendline for each of the chemical species involved in this equilibrium to show their changes in concentration over time. Include a key.
questions.answer:
- **0–5 min:** $[\text{A}_2]$ falls from 1.4 to 1.2 mol L$^{-1}$ (a change of 0.2), so by the 1 : 2 : 2 mole ratio $[\text{B}_2]$ falls by 0.4 from 1.0 to 0.6 mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{AB}_2]$ rises by 0.4 from 0 to 0.4 mol L$^{-1}$. The curves are steepest at the start and flatten off (rate slows) as equilibrium is reached at 5 min.
- **5–10 min:** all three lines are horizontal (equilibrium).
- **10–15 min:** the forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right. There is no sudden jump; $[\text{A}_2]$ and $[\text{B}_2]$ decrease gradually and $[\text{AB}_2]$ increases gradually, in the ratio 1 : 2 : 2 (e.g. $\text{A}_2$ 1.2 → 1.1, $\text{B}_2$ 0.6 → 0.4, $\text{AB}_2$ 0.4 → 0.6 mol L$^{-1}$).
- **15–20 min:** all lines horizontal again (new equilibrium).

questions.question:
Gases $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ react according to the equation:

$$\text{A}_2(g) + 2\text{B}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{AB}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$

A mixture of $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ was placed into a sealed vessel. The initial concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.4 mol L$^{-1}$ and the initial concentration of $\text{B}_2$ was 1.0 mol L$^{-1}$. At 5 minutes, the system had reached equilibrium where the concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.2 mol L$^{-1}$. The system remained at equilibrium until at 10 minutes the temperature of the system was reduced. At 15 minutes, the system re-established equilibrium.

Calculate $K_{eq}$ at 7 minutes.
questions.answer:
At 7 minutes the system is at the first equilibrium: $[\text{A}_2] = 1.2$, $[\text{B}_2] = 1.0 - 2(0.2) = 0.6$ and $[\text{AB}_2] = 2(0.2) = 0.4$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{AB}_2]^2}{[\text{A}_2][\text{B}_2]^2} = \frac{0.4^2}{1.2 \times 0.6^2} = 0.37$$

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. Draw the structural formulae of the products formed in the reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol.
questions.answer:
The products are ethyl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (the ester), and water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$:

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. What reagent could be added to act as a catalyst for this reaction?
questions.answer: A few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid.

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. Identify a laboratory technique that could be used to help this reaction reach equilibrium quicker and provide another advantage of using this technique.
questions.answer: Refluxing — heating the mixture with a vertical condenser fitted to the flask — allows the mixture to be heated (increasing the reaction rate) for a long time. Another advantage is that volatile (and flammable) reactants and products condense and return to the flask instead of escaping, so no material is lost and the risk of fire from vapours is reduced.

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.034 \times 0.50 = 0.017$ mol, so $n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})_{eq} = 0.017$ mol (1 : 1 reaction).

$[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]_{eq} = 0.017/0.100 = 0.17$ mol L$^{-1}$; initially $[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}] = [\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}] = 0.050/0.100 = 0.50$ mol L$^{-1}$.

| | $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ | $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ | $\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.50 | 0.50 | 0 |
| Change | $-0.33$ | $-0.33$ | $+0.33$ |
| Equilibrium | 0.17 | 0.17 | 0.33 |

Treating water as the solvent (so it is left out of the expression):

$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}][\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}]} = \frac{0.33}{0.17^2} = 11$$

*(If water is instead treated as a product, $[\text{H}_2\text{O}] = 0.33$ mol L$^{-1}$ is included and $K_{eq} = \dfrac{0.33^2}{0.17^2} = 3.8$; the school's marking guidelines used the first approach.)*

questions.question:
The structural diagram shows a section of polymer A:

$$-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-$$

Draw the monomers for polymer A.
questions.answer: Polymer A is a polyester formed by condensation polymerisation. Its monomers are the diol propane-1,3-diol, $\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$, and the dicarboxylic acid propanedioic acid, $\text{HOOC}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$.

questions.question:
The structural diagram shows a section of polymer A:

$$-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-$$

The monomers of polymer A are propane-1,3-diol ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$) and propanedioic acid ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$). Determine the molar mass of a section of polymer A that consists of 40 monomers.
questions.answer:
$M(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_2) = 3(12.01) + 8(1.008) + 2(16.00) = 76.094$ g mol$^{-1}$

$M(\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4) = 3(12.01) + 4(1.008) + 4(16.00) = 104.062$ g mol$^{-1}$

40 monomers = 20 of each, alternating. Joining 40 monomers in a chain forms 39 ester links, each eliminating one water molecule ($M = 18.016$):

$$M = 20(76.094 + 104.062) - 39(18.016) = 3603.12 - 702.62 = 2900\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

(Equivalently: 20 repeating units of 144.124 g mol$^{-1}$ plus H and OH on the chain ends: $20(144.124) + 18.016 = 2900$ g mol$^{-1}$.)

questions.question:
A reaction flow chart is described below. Complete it by answering each part.

- But-2-ene reacts with reagent X to form $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$.
- $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$ reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ to form compound D.
- Compound D reacts with reagent Y to form butan-2-one.
- Propanal reacts with reagent Z to form $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$.
- $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ reacts with $\text{NH}_3$ to form compound E.
- $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ reacts with compound D to form compound F.

Identify reagents X, Y and Z; draw the structural formula and give the IUPAC name of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$, D, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ and E; and draw the structural formula of F.
questions.answer:
- **Reagent X:** hydrogen bromide, HBr.
- **$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$:** $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, 2-bromobutane.
- **D:** substitution of Br by OH gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, butan-2-ol.
- **Reagent Y:** acidified potassium permanganate ($\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-$) or acidified potassium dichromate ($\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$) — oxidises the secondary alcohol to the ketone.
- **Reagent Z:** acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ or acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ (oxidises the aldehyde).
- **$\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$:** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, propanoic acid.
- **E:** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$, propanamide.
- **F:** the ester formed from propanoic acid and butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}-\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (butan-2-yl propanoate).

*(The original paper printed the bromoalkane as $\text{C}_4\text{H}_7\text{Br}$; addition of HBr to but-2-ene gives $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$, as in the marking guidelines' answer 2-bromobutane, so the formula has been corrected.)*
